notes.body:
The English phrase "that posture" is actually translating على الحجة directly, and **no sleeping position is named before it** in the passage — the word "that" creates a false impression of a back-reference where none exists.

What الحجة means here emerges from **the structure of the whole prohibition**. Three positions are listed:

- على الحجة — the one the English renders as "that posture"
- على وجهه — face-down, the prone position
- على ظهرها — flat on the back, for women specifically

Because face-down and back-lying are each named separately, على الحجة must refer to something distinct from both. The most defensible reading — consistent with the well-known teaching that the right side is the recommended sleep position — is that it means the **left side**. Sleeping on the left places the body's full weight on the heart, which classical Islamic medicine considered harmful; the right side was preferred because it eases the heart and mirrors the position of one lying in the grave, facing the قبلة.

The prohibition does not end there. Maulana Ali gives the face-down position **its own sharper emphasis** — "whomever you see sleeping on his face, wake him" — making the prone posture the most urgent concern of the three. The passage draws a complete map of positions to avoid, leaving the right side as the one good posture implied by everything it forbids.

etymology: الحجة: from root ح-ج-ج, meaning to repair purposefully toward a destination. This yields الحجّ (the pilgrimage — the intentional journey) and حجة (the compelling proof — the argument that drives decisively to its conclusion). In على الحجة as a sleeping posture, the most defensible reading is the left side, where the body's weight presses directly upon the heart.

العيادة: from root ع-و-د, meaning to return or come back. The same root gives عيد (the recurring festival — the day that returns) and عود (the return itself). To visit the sick (العيادة) is to return to your brother in his most vulnerable hour — the word carries within it the idea of faithful, repeated coming-back.

البلاء: from root ب-ل-و, meaning to test something by subjecting it to use until its true quality is revealed. The root also yields بلي (to wear out, to decay under pressure). Affliction (البلاء) in this tradition is therefore a refining test — it does not simply punish; it wears away the outer layer and exposes what is genuinely within.

notes.body:
The chapter intends both readings, and that double weight is the whole point. The **opening claim** targets the living wailer: to engage in wailing (النوح) is to call down upon oneself the very conditions through which spiritual punishment moves. The story of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah reveals exactly where those conditions also land. He sees an angel standing over him, the dying man himself, swinging a flaming iron mace toward his head with every shriek the women around him raise.

The Prophet's closing words seal the second reading.

> صَدَقَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ فَمَا بَالُ مَوْتَاكُمْ يُبْتَلَوْنَ بِقَوْلِ أَحْيَائِكُمْ
> 'Abdullah has spoken the truth. What is the matter with your dead, that they should be made to suffer by the words of your living?

The rebuke is aimed at the living, but **the suffering falls on the dead**. The soul crossing from this world to the next is stripped of the body's ordinary protections at exactly the moment it is most exposed — and the wailing of the living reaches into that crossing. It is not the dead man's own sin that brings the angel's mace down; it is the living mourners' sin, still moving along the cord that has not yet gone cold between them.

The harm to the wailer is equally exact: whoever strikes his thigh at a calamity (المصيبة) **forfeits his reward** outright, and the two accursed voices draw Allah's hatred onto the one who raises them. The wailer damages their own soul in the same moment they harm the one they have lost.

The living wailer and the departing soul are two ends of a cord the wailing tears at from both directions at once.

etymology: النوح (wailing): from root ن-و-ح, meaning to moan with a sustained, drawn-out sound. The root suggests continuous public outpouring — not a single cry but a prolonged, rhythmic lament. النوح names the prohibited form: not quiet tears but performed, sustained grief that has crossed the line into display.

العويل (lamentation): from root ع-و-ل, meaning to cry out in dependency and need. The same root gives عيال — household dependents, those who lean on another. العويل is the cry of someone who has lost their support. That etymology tells you why it so easily becomes desperate and uncontrolled: it is the sound of felt helplessness.

البكاء (weeping): from root ب-ك-و, meaning to shed tears — quietly, organically. The root carries the sense of tears simply flowing, not shaped into performance. This is the grief the Prophet permitted and modeled himself: natural, involuntary, tender. البكاء and النوح look alike from the outside but are spiritually worlds apart.

المصيبة (calamity): from root ص-و-ب, meaning to strike a target accurately. A مصيبة is literally 'that which hits its mark' — calamity conceived not as random misfortune but as a precise stroke. The root also gives أصاب (to hit truly, to be correct). Calamity in Arabic is not scattered noise — it is aimed.
